dedication.title: This book belongs to

titlePage.by: A workbook for mother, partner and family

howTo.title: How to use this book
howTo.intro: Each week has five small invitations — for your mind, body, heart, spirit and plate. Every one was chosen because it can support your baby’s growth through your wellbeing, closeness and senses, and help calm your mind. Do what feels good. Skip freely. Little and often is better than perfect.
strands: Read, talk, sing, chant or tell a story — your voice is baby’s first music.
Journal, gratitude, letters to baby, and a partner task.
Colour, trace, gaze, rest your hands in a mudrā, or sit in silence.
A brain-supportive food of the week with a simple Indian recipe and food-safety notes.
badges: Science-backed: supported by good studies or major guidelines (nutrition, sleep, stress reduction, safe movement, talking and singing to baby).
Emerging evidence: early or modest research, mostly about the mother’s calm (music, mantra, meditation, bonding).
Tradition & culture: India’s heritage shared with respect and its source named — not a medical claim.
howTo.times: Time chips show roughly how long an activity takes: 2, 5, 10 or 20 minutes.
howTo.checkin: At the bottom of each week: circle your mood, note sleep, baby’s movements, water and energy, and take one calm minute.
howTo.promise: This book never promises a ‘genius’, a particular look, or a boy or a girl. It offers care, calm and connection — which is what babies and mothers truly need.

medical.title: A note on health, safety and respect
paras: This book is for wellbeing and connection. It does not replace antenatal care. Please attend all your check-ups, take the supplements your doctor prescribes, and ask before starting any new physical activity, breathing practice or diet change.

Every BODY and NOURISH activity carries two reminders: Check with your doctor first, and Stop if… Some pregnancies need extra care — for example with bleeding, a low-lying placenta, twins, high blood pressure, diabetes or a history of early labour. Your doctor will tell you what is right for you.

Breath practices here are gentle only. We do not include breath-holding (kumbhaka), kapālabhāti, bhastrikā, inversions, deep backbends, lying on the belly, hot yoga, or herbal and Ayurvedic medicines — these are not safe to self-prescribe in pregnancy.

Classical texts are shared as heritage. Where they describe diets, herbs or procedures, we summarise them as history only. Some old customs are based on fear (such as eclipse restrictions); they have no scientific basis and are not included.

Choosing or predicting a baby’s sex is illegal in India (PC&PNDT Act, 1994) and has no basis in science. Nothing in this book — no ritual, food or chant — affects a baby’s sex, skin colour, looks or intelligence.
medical.inclusive: Rooted in India, open to all. This book draws on Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and folk traditions of India, and it welcomes families of every faith and of none. Every spiritual activity has a secular alternative (next page). Use what speaks to you; leave the rest with a smile.
medical.disclaimer: Disclaimer: The authors and publishers accept no liability for the use of this book. Information is general and may not suit every pregnancy. Content flagged for review should be checked by an obstetrician, an Ayurvedic physician and a Sanskrit scholar before distribution.

path.title: Choose your own path
path.intro: Every spiritual practice in this book has an equal, secular twin. The calming effect mostly comes from slow breath, gentle attention and loving connection — available to everyone.
rows: A favourite poem or prayer of your own faith, read slowly
A lullaby from your own family
Soft gaze at a flower or geometric pattern
Hands resting on your belly while you breathe
Counted breathing (4 in, 6 out) / humming a tune
levels: Keeps the art, mudrās and peace mantras; cakra and yantra practices become their secular twins.
Every spiritual activity is replaced by its twin. Rebuild the book with the ‘secular’ setting.

warning.title: When to call your doctor immediately
warning.sub: Go to hospital or call for help straight away if you notice any of these. Do not wait until morning.
signs: Bleeding or spotting from the vagina, at any stage
Fluid leaking or gushing from the vagina
Baby moving less, differently, or not at all (from about 24 weeks)
Severe headache, blurred vision or seeing spots
Sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet
High fever (38 °C / 100.4 °F or more), or fever with chills
Severe or continuing pain in the belly, or regular tightening before 37 weeks
Vomiting so much you cannot keep water down
Difficulty breathing, chest pain or a racing heart
Pain, redness or swelling in one calf
Burning or pain when passing urine, or foul-smelling discharge
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, or feeling unable to cope
warning.instinct: Trust your instinct. If something feels wrong, it is always right to call.
warning.src: Based on the MoHFW Mother & Child Protection Card (2018), WHO (2016) and ACOG (2020). Numbers to be re-checked before printing.

journey.title: Your journey: what science sees
journey.sub: How your baby’s senses and brain develop across the three trimesters
rows: Neural tube forms and closes by week 6; brain regions begin.
Rapid growth of nerve cells; brain grows larger and more active.
Surface folds into ridges; connections multiply — and keep growing for years after birth.
First responses to sound around 19 weeks; low tones first.
Knows familiar voices; newborns prefer their mother’s voice.
Mouth area responds to touch around 8 weeks.
Responds to touch all over; moves more when you stroke your belly.
Grasps, sucks thumb, explores the face and cord.
Swallows amniotic fluid, which carries flavours of your food.
May later accept flavours met in the womb more easily.
Tiny movements from about week 7 (not felt).
Strong kicks; a pattern you can learn. Movements should not slow down before birth.
journey.foot: Sources: Hepper & Shahidullah 1994; DeCasper & Fifer 1980; Kisilevsky 2003; Marx & Nagy 2015; Mennella 2001; RCOG 2011; Moore, The Developing Human.

sages.title: What the sages observed
sages.sub: Classical Indian descriptions of the growing baby, beside modern findings. Shared as heritage — the ancient texts and modern science use different methods and should not be equated.
rows: Garbha Upaniṣad: after one night a jelly (kalala), after seven nights a bubble. Caraka: kalala.
Fertilisation, implantation; three cell layers form.
Caraka: becomes solid (ghana). Garbha Up.: the head forms.
Neural tube closes; heart beats; limb buds.
Caraka: all limbs and senses appear together. Garbha Up.: the feet.
Fetal period begins; organs formed; fingers and toes.
Suśruta: the heart becomes manifest; the mother is ‘two-hearted’ and has cravings (dauhṛda).
Heartbeat easily heard; baby moves arms and legs.
Suśruta: the mind (manas) becomes more awake.
Flutters felt; first responses to sound.
Rapid brain growth; responds to touch and sound.
Suśruta: all limbs clearly formed. Garbha Up.: quickened with life.
Fat stores, lungs maturing; brain surface folds.
Garbha Up.: complete in every part.
Full term from 37 weeks; ready to meet you.
sages.foot: Sources: Caraka Saṃhitā Śārīrasthāna 4; Suśruta Saṃhitā Śārīrasthāna 3; Garbha Upaniṣad. Verse references need verification by a Sanskrit scholar.

gs.title: What is Garbha Saṃskāra?
paras: Garbha means womb and saṃskāra means a refining rite or impression. Together, garbha saṃskāra names India’s old and living idea that a mother’s food, feelings, surroundings and sounds matter to the child she carries — and that a pregnancy deserves care, celebration and calm.

Ayurveda’s classical texts — the Caraka and Suśruta Saṃhitās (roughly 2,000 years old) — describe garbhiṇī paricaryā, care of the pregnant woman. Suśruta advises that from the very first day she should be ‘ever joyful, clean, adorned, dressed in light clothes, and devoted to peace and auspicious acts’. Modern research on maternal stress agrees that a mother’s wellbeing matters.

Today the National Institute of Ayurveda (Ministry of AYUSH) teaches garbha saṃskāra as care through diet, lifestyle, yoga, meditation, mantra and music, complementing — not replacing — modern antenatal care.
samskara: Rite around conception — here, simply a heartfelt intention (saṅkalpa).

An old 3rd-month rite that once wished for a son. We reject that aim: sex selection is illegal (PC&PNDT Act) and unscientific. Many families now mark the month with a blessing for a healthy child — whoever they are.
The parting of the mother’s hair with music and blessings (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.14) — ancestor of godh bharai, sīmantham, valaikāppu, sādh and dohāḷe jevaṇ.
gs.promiseTitle: What this book will never claim
promise: That any practice raises IQ or creates a ‘genius’
That skin colour, looks or height can be shaped
That anything can choose or predict a boy or a girl
gs.foot: Some modern programmes have made such claims; they have been widely criticised as unscientific. Sources: Suśruta Śā. 10/3; NIA 2024; Pandey 1969.

tve.title: Tradition & evidence
tve.intro: Our ancestors noticed much that science now confirms: babies hear in the womb; a mother’s calm matters; good food and rest are foundations. Other beliefs have not been tested, or were based on fear. Here is an honest map.
rows: Babies hear and learn familiar voices in the womb.
Proven (from ~19–24 weeks). It builds familiarity, not intelligence.
A mother’s calm and support matter.
Good food, rest and gentle movement.
Strong evidence — plus iron, folate, iodine and food safety.
Music, mantra, meditation, yoga for calm.
Encouraging but small or mixed studies — for the mother.
Contemplative and cultural — no medical effect claimed.
No evidence; harmful or illegal — not included.

kosha.title: Pañca Kośa — five layers of care
kosha.sub: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.1–2.5) describes five ‘sheaths’, from the body inward to joy. We use them as a gentle self-care check-in.
rows: What does my body need today: rest, water, food, movement?
Is my breath easy? Three slow breaths.
What am I feeling? Name it kindly.
What do I know is true for me and baby?
kosha.foot: In the Upaniṣad this is a teaching on the Self; here it is offered as a simple framework for care. (✦ Tradition & culture)

chakra.title: The seven cakras — a symbolic map
chakra.sub: Use this map to check in with your feelings. It comes from the tantric tradition (Ṣaṭ-cakra-nirūpaṇa, 1577) — it is symbolic, not anatomy, and not a medical system. The rainbow colours are a modern convention.
rows: I am part of something larger than me.
My voice is my baby’s first song.
My heart has room for us both.
I have the strength I need, one day at a time.
I flow with the changes in my body.
I am safe, supported and held.

mudra.title: Mudrās — gentle hand gestures
mudra.sub: Hand gestures from ritual, classical dance and meditation. Rest the hands comfortably and breathe slowly for 2 minutes. Healing claims made for mudrās are not proven — enjoy them as a way to focus and settle.
items: Tips of thumb and index finger touch; other fingers relaxed.
Steady attention; a classic meditation gesture.
Right hand resting in the left, palms up, thumbs touching, in the lap.
Thumb tip touches the middle fingertip.
Thumb touches the tips of the ring and little fingers.
Thumb touches the tips of the middle and ring fingers.
Traditionally kept for the last weeks (from about 36 weeks) — a custom only; the gesture itself is harmless.
mudra.foot: ✦ Tradition & culture · Secular twin: rest your hands on your belly and breathe.

yantra.title: Yantras & the Śrī Yantra
paras: A yantra is a geometric diagram for contemplation. The most celebrated is the Śrī Yantra (Śrī Cakra) of the Śrī Vidyā tradition: nine interlocking triangles — four pointing up and five pointing down — weave together to form 43 smaller triangles around a central point, the bindu. Around them bloom lotuses of eight and sixteen petals, three circles and a square ‘gateway’ (bhūpura).

The upward and downward triangles are traditionally read as the meeting of Śiva and Śakti — consciousness and creative energy. Many see in it an image of creation itself: a whole universe unfolding from a single point. For a mother, it can be a quiet picture of life growing from a seed.
Drawing the Śrī Yantra accurately is famously difficult: several lines must meet at exactly the same points. The yantra on the next page was calculated by computer to meet these conditions closely.
how: Sit comfortably with the yantra at eye level, about an arm’s length away.
Rest your eyes softly on the central dot. Blink whenever you need to.
After 1–3 minutes, close your eyes and rest, palms over the eyes if you like.
yantra.safety: Never strain or stare. Blink normally; stop if your eyes water or ache. No candle-gazing for long periods.
yantra.foot: ✦ Tradition & culture · Secular twin: soft gaze at a flower or a geometric pattern. Sources: Śrī Vidyā tradition; Kulaichev 1984.

yantraPage.title: Śrī Yantra — trace & colour
yantraPage.sub: Trace the triangles slowly with a pencil, then colour from the outside in. End by resting your gaze at the centre.

kolam.title: Kolam & rangoli — lines around dots
paras: Every dawn across South India, women draw kolam at the threshold with rice flour — loops woven around a grid of dots (pulli). Rangoli (Maharashtra, Gujarat), alpana (Bengal), muggulu (Andhra & Telangana) and mandana (Rajasthan) are its cousins. Mathematicians have studied kolam as elegant closed curves; families see them as welcome, beauty and care.
Trace the patterns below, then try your own on the empty grid. One continuous line, looping around the dots, slow and unhurried. A wobble is part of the beauty.
kolam.foot: ✦ Tradition & culture · ◐ Repetitive drawing may help calm attention.

sound.title: Sound & mantra
sound.sub: How to chant — or hum — safely and calmly
how: Breathe in gently through the nose — never strain.
Let the sound ride on a slow out-breath; then breathe normally.
Never hold the breath. Use a soft voice. Stop if dizzy or tired.
3, 5 or 9 repetitions are plenty. Silence afterwards is part of the practice.
key: a soft echo of breath: śāntiḥ ≈ ‘shaantihi’
both ‘sh’; ṣ with tongue curled back
sound.evidence: What the research says: chanting and humming slow the breath and lengthen the exhalation, which is linked with calm. Studies are small (an fMRI pilot of Oṃ chanting; a very-low-quality review of bhrāmarī). There is no evidence that mantras shape a baby’s character or intelligence — their gift is a calmer, more connected mother. (◐ Emerging evidence)

lullabyNote: Lullabies are public domain, traditional refrains or original compositions written for this book. Native-script text should be checked by native speakers.
storiesIntro: Original retellings to read aloud. Folk stories are labelled as such.

nourish.title: Nourish — food for two
nourish.sub: Brain-supportive nutrients and where to find them in Indian kitchens
rows: Forms the brain and spine early
Dals, rajma, chana, palak, methi, oranges, peanuts
Blood for two; baby’s iron stores
Green leafy vegetables, bajra, ragi, poha, dates, halim (garden cress)
Soya, paneer, milk, peanuts, rajma, cauliflower
Brain and eyes; lowers early-birth risk
Walnuts, flaxseed, chia, mustard oil (ALA — ask about DHA)
Dals, sprouts (cooked), paneer, curd, soya, nuts
Milk, curd, ragi, til, paneer, leafy greens
Milk, curd, paneer; ask about a supplement
do: Boiled or pasteurised milk and paneer
Eggs, meat and fish fully cooked
Wash fruit and vegetables in clean running water
Take the iron, folic acid and calcium tablets your doctor prescribes — at separate times
dont: Alcohol or tobacco in any form (including gutka and second-hand smoke)
Raw or half-boiled eggs, raw sprouts, raw milk
High-mercury fish (shark, swordfish, king mackerel, big-eye tuna)
Street food made with untreated water or ice
Herbal medicines, kadhas, rasāyanas or supplements without your doctor
Fasting or ‘eating for two’ — extra needs are modest (about 350 kcal a day from the 2nd trimester)
nourish.foot: Sources: ICMR-NIN 2020 & 2024; WHO 2016; Middleton 2018; Caudill 2018; FDA/EPA 2021; ACOG 2010. Quantities to be checked with your doctor or dietitian.

masa.title: Traditional month-wise care
masa.sub: Māsānumāsika paricaryā — a summary of classical Ayurvedic texts
masa.warn: This is a summary of historical texts. It is NOT medical or dietary advice. Your needs depend on your health — discuss any change in diet with your doctor.
rows: Plain milk, as desired, with wholesome food
Butter from milk, or milk with butter
Rice gruel cooked in milk with ghee (kṣīra-yavāgū)
Like a light kheer or daliya (recipe in week 34)
Procedures are medical — not part of this book
masa.thread: The common thread: warm, gentle, nourishing food, easy to digest, with the mother’s appetite and wishes respected. Suśruta (Śā. 10/4) and Vāgbhaṭa give similar month-wise lists. Modern guidance adds iron, folate, iodine, DHA and food safety — follow your doctor’s advice.
masa.foot: Sources: Caraka Saṃhitā Śā. 8/32; Suśruta Saṃhitā Śā. 10/4; Aṣṭāṅga Saṅgraha Śā. 3 (verse references need verification).

name: Bīja
बीज
The Seed
1.text: A time of beginnings. Your body is doing enormous, invisible work. Rest, nourish, and be gentle with yourself — nausea and tiredness are signs of growth, not weakness.

name: Aṅkura
अङ्कुर
The Sprout
2.text: Often the most comfortable trimester. Baby begins to hear around 19 weeks, and you may feel the first flutters. Your voice becomes part of baby’s world.
focus: Talking, reading and singing to baby

name: Puṣpa
पुष्प
The Bloom
3.text: Baby grows fast and gets ready for the world. Go to sleep on your side, learn your baby’s movement pattern, and gather your circle of support.

moon: Candra — the cool, calm light. Colour slowly; let each ring be one breath.
flower: Puṣpa — blossoming. Choose three colours and repeat them around the circle.
own: Begin at the centre dot. Repeat a shape around each ring until it feels complete.
reflect: What I want to carry into the next weeks

daily.title: Daily rhythm

morning.title: Morning calm (10 minutes)
steps: On waking, lie on your side; three slow breaths.
A glass of water; a light snack if nauseous.
Say good morning to baby by name.
Choose one intention (saṅkalpa) for the day.

evening.title: Evening wind-down (20 minutes)
steps: Warm bath or wash; loose, comfortable clothes.
Same story, same song for baby.
Three good things — said aloud or written.
Go to sleep on your side, pillow between the knees (essential from 28 weeks).

daily.note: Waking on your back is not a cause for alarm — simply turn onto your side. Sources: ACOG 2020; Cronin 2019.

playlist.title: Sound-bath playlist
playlist.ideas: Ideas: rain, birdsong, flute, veena, sitar ālāp, soft bhajans, a grandparent singing, ocean waves, your family’s lullaby.
playlist.safety: Keep the volume comfortable. Never place headphones on your belly.
talk: Good morning! Today the weather is…
This is the sound of your father’s / mother’s / grandmother’s voice…
I am cooking… can you smell the jeera?
Your family is waiting for you. Your name might be…
Let me tell you about the place where you will live…
Goodnight. I love you. See you tomorrow.

family.title: Partner & family
partner: Come to at least one scan or check-up each trimester.
Take over cooking or cleaning on tired days.
Learn the warning signs (page 8) and the movement rule.
Talk, read or sing to the bump every evening.
Give a foot or hand massage once a week.
Pack the hospital bag together; plan transport.
Protect her rest — be the gatekeeper for visitors.
grand: Teach a family lullaby or story (page 73).
Share the family’s memories for the family tree.
Offer a blessing — and practical help.
Gently let go of old fears and taboos — reassure, don’t restrict.

tree.title: Our family tree
tree.sub: Fill in names, places and one word about each person.

celebrate.title: Celebration planner
celebrate.sub: Godh bharai · Sīmantham · Valaikāppu · Sādh · Dohāḷe jevaṇ · Baby shower
celebrate.intro: Descended from the Vedic sīmantonnayana — when blessings and music surrounded the mother. Celebration only: let the mother sit, eat and enjoy. Please no sex-prediction games, rituals or remarks.

kicks.title: Know your baby’s movements
kicks.sub: From 28 weeks. There is no ‘right number’ of kicks — learn what is normal for YOUR baby.
kicks.how: Each day, note when baby is most active (morning / afternoon / evening / night) and tick if movements felt normal. If you are unsure, lie on your left side and focus on movements for up to 2 hours.
kicks.alert: If movements slow down, change or stop — do not wait until tomorrow. Call your doctor or hospital now. Do not rely on home Dopplers or apps.

bag.title: Hospital bag & home-ready checklist
mother: MCP card, reports, ID, insurance papers
Snacks (chikki, dry fruit) and water bottle
baby: Soft cotton clothes ×4, caps, mittens, socks
home: A clean, safe place for baby to sleep (on the back, firm flat surface)
Help arranged for the first weeks
Thermometer; doctor and hospital numbers on the fridge

birth.title: Birth preferences
birth.sub: Talk these through with your doctor; birth can be unpredictable — flexibility is part of the plan.
items: Movement and positions I’d like to try
Comfort measures (breathing, music, massage, warm water)
Pain relief I’d like to discuss
If a caesarean is needed, I’d like…
After birth: skin-to-skin, delayed cord clamping (discuss)
Feeding: start within the first hour
Anything about my faith or culture to respect

newborn.title: First weeks with baby
feed: Start breastfeeding within the first hour if possible; skin-to-skin helps.
Feed on demand — 8–12 times a day in the early weeks.
Exclusive breastfeeding for six months is recommended (WHO).
Ask your nurse, ASHA or a lactation counsellor for help early — it is common to need it.
newborn.vacc: Follow the vaccination schedule on your Mother & Child Protection Card. Birth doses usually include BCG, OPV-0 and Hepatitis B.
newborn.dangerTitle: Newborn danger signs — go to a doctor immediately
danger: Not feeding well, or unable to suck
Fast breathing or chest drawing in with each breath
Fever, or feels cold to touch
Yellow skin in the first 24 hours, or yellow palms and soles
Redness, pus or bleeding from the cord stump
Vomiting everything; very few wet nappies
newborn.sleep: Safe sleep: baby on the back, on a firm flat surface, nothing loose around the face.

names.title: Name ideas
names.sub: Names, meanings and why we love them. (Nāmakaraṇa — the naming ceremony — is traditionally held around the 11th or 12th day.)
names.seeds: Some ideas: Aarav (peaceful), Aditi (boundless), Anaya (caring), Ira (earth), Kabir (great), Kavya (poetry), Mira (light, ocean), Nila (blue), Omkar (sacred sound), Tara (star), Vihaan (dawn), Zoya (alive).

met.title: The day we met
lines: The first thing I noticed about you
The first song we sang to you

tveFull.title: Tradition vs evidence — at a glance
rows: Keep the mother cheerful and calm (Suśruta Śā. 10/3).
Maternal stress, anxiety and depression are linked with child outcomes; support and stress-reduction help mothers.
The baby hears and learns in the womb (Abhimanyu, Prahlāda).
Yes for hearing: from ~19–24 weeks; newborns recognise mother’s voice and familiar passages. No evidence of learning skills or knowledge.
Mantra chanting purifies or shapes the child.
Chanting and humming may calm the mother (slower breathing; small studies). No evidence of effects on a child’s character or intelligence.
Month-wise milk, ghee and nourishing foods.
Adequate energy, protein and calcium matter; modern care adds iron, folate, iodine, DHA, B12 and food safety. Exact month-wise formulas are untested.
Cravings are common and mostly harmless; craving clay, chalk or ice (pica) can signal iron deficiency — tell your doctor.
Social support protects maternal mental health.
Generally safe when adapted; benefits for stress and labour, with low-quality evidence. Avoid inversions, hot yoga and breath-holding.
No physiological evidence; valuable as contemplative, artistic and cultural practice.
No evidence; they increase fear and can restrict care. Not included.
Not tested for safety in pregnancy; some products contain heavy metals (Saper 2008). Not included.
Sex selection is illegal (PC&PNDT Act) and impossible by ritual. Reframed as a blessing for any child.
A much-loved folk tale (a later addition to the epic) — not a historical or medical account.
